sourceText: The name on the threshold was MIEVILLE-TWIN-CITY. Beneath it, in smaller letters, was the dedication: China Miéville — The City & The City. It was not a reproduction of a book but a world built around the question the book had made impossible to forget. Two jurisdictions occupy the same geography, and their citizens are trained not to see the other world. The memorial bore the name of China Miéville — The City & The City precisely to keep the genealogy of the idea visible. Aster considered it indecent for a late civilization to treat the imagination of the past as anonymous ore: authors did not own the futures, but they deserved to remain on the map as points of intellectual origin. The children had quickly learned that a wormhole is also a trade treaty, and an additional dimension is also a method for walking through prison walls. Vela tracked the differences erased by elegant explanations. For her, two worlds that produced the same statistic did not thereby become the same world. The children were met by Iska, who refused demonstrations. ‘If you can perform miracles, perform them after you tell me what 101 becomes irreversible.’ Marae appreciated the formulation; Aster admitted that in earlier eras she herself would have asked the question only after optimizing. The problem closed quickly around them: Marae saves a person physically beside her, violating a border that exists chiefly in perception. There was no clean option. Every intervention shifted the cost between persons, eras, or definitions of personhood; and refusing to intervene was itself a choice made by those who could leave. Kesh opened the analytical layer of the Table for a few seconds. The active cells were Ct — Topological City: the border is perceptual and legal; Sp — Perceptual Separation: borders are maintained through disciplined perception. Course references included China Miéville — The City & The City; China Miéville. The rule was strict: naming a work did not substitute for an explanation. They had to identify the mechanism that could migrate into another story and the consequences that could not be copied without remainder. Marae broke the first consensus. ‘Do not tell me what their model prefers. Ask them, and bear the time their answer takes.’ Orin answered without raising their voice: ‘I do not want the perfect branch. I want us to know what we sacrificed in order to call it perfect.’ It was not a pedagogical quarrel. Over the last nights, the children’s differences had become incompatible political programs. Aster felt the Hunger precisely when an explanation closed too elegantly. A perfect theory reduced surprise, and surprise was the last symptom that something before her had not yet become part of her. 102 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS The children had noticed that their disagreement calmed her more than any extravagant universe did. Vela evaluated the solution not by efficiency but by the differences it made invisible. She found one: a local minority for whom the proposed “improvement” destroyed a practice with no equivalent. Optimizing the average concealed a small and perfectly legal extinction. The night did not end in victory. The Table notes that a new world can arise without new matter, solely from a rule about what one is permitted to recognize. Aster recorded the decision in the world’s provenance register and, more importantly, allowed its inhabitants to contest it. For several eras she had been learning something that seems banal to lesser powers: technical reversibility is not the same as biographical reversibility. While Kesh closed the record, Tern compared the sector’s noise with the anomaly detected in the Vinge zone. The pattern reappeared, but only in worlds where Aster’s control weakened. The correlation was unpleasant: either someone was calling him from outside, or his own need for an outside was learning to forge evidence. For the course, Kesh also linked the night to the ALTERATION operator. In the Table, periodicity did not mean that the same objects reappeared, but that the same operation — changes the value or form of an existing rule without yet changing the kind of thing on which it operates — could recur across different families. Thus a copy of a body, a copy of a mind, a copy of a world, and a copy of a history were not the same phenomenon, but they shared a conceptual chemistry. 103 Vela introduced the propagation test: if you remove the speculative idea and nothing in the institutions, relationships, or vocabulary has to be rewritten, the idea has remained scenery. Kesh introduced the opposite test: if the idea seems to explain every detail, you have overcompressed the world. Between the two tests lay the region in which an element became fertile without becoming superstition. Marae added the refusal test. Who can say “no,” and what happens afterward? In universes with near-divine technology, that question often separated an instrument from a regime. A power that treats refusal as a data error can be benevolent in intention and totalitarian in structure. When the threshold closed, Aster remained silent one second longer than protocol required. The children had already noticed that this was her smallest unit of fear. 104 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS
